tf.statement: If two events have positive probabilities and are mutually exclusive, then they are independent.
tf.explanation: Mutual exclusivity gives \(P(A\cap B)=0\), whereas independence would require \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)>0\).

tf.statement: For events with \(P(A),P(B)>0\), the identity \(P(A\mid B)=P(B\mid A)\) holds even when the prior probabilities differ.
tf.explanation: Bayes' rule gives \(P(A\mid B)/P(B\mid A)=P(A)/P(B)\) when the common joint probability is positive. For example, \(B\subset A\) can make the two conditional probabilities different.

tf.statement: For a random variable with a probability density, the density value \(p(x)\) may exceed one even though \(P(X=x)=0\).
tf.explanation: A density is integrated to obtain probabilities. A uniform variable on \((0,1/4)\) has density \(4\) there, and every singleton has probability zero.
Linearity of expectation needs existence of the relevant expectations, not independence. Independence is relevant to factoring product expectations and eliminating covariance terms.
Expand the centered difference and take expectations; the cross term has a minus sign.

tf.statement: If two variables each have a normal marginal distribution and have zero covariance, they must be independent.
tf.explanation: The sufficient condition is joint Gaussianity. Let \(Z\sim N(0,1)\) and let an independent sign \(R\) equal \(\pm1\) with equal probabilities. Then \(X=Z\) and \(Y=RZ\) each are standard normal and have covariance zero, but \(|X|=|Y|\), so they are dependent. This states the qualification needed for the normal-variable claim on the slide.

tf.statement: For iid observations with finite variance \(\sigma^2\), the variance of their sample mean is \(\sigma^2/n\).
tf.explanation: The mean has weights \(1/n\); independence eliminates all off-diagonal covariance terms, giving \(n\sigma^2/n^2\).

tf.statement: The weak law of large numbers says that, for a sufficiently large finite sample, the sample mean equals the population mean with probability one.
tf.explanation: The law concerns convergence in probability: for each fixed \(\epsilon>0\), \(P(|\bar X_n-\mu|>\epsilon)\to0\). It does not assert exact equality at a finite sample size.

tf.statement: For iid nonnormal observations with finite positive variance, the central limit theorem makes the standardized sample mean exactly standard normal at every finite sample size.
tf.explanation: The central limit theorem gives a limiting distribution, hence a large-sample approximation. Exact finite-sample normality follows when the observations themselves are iid normal.

tf.statement: If \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_k\) are independent standard normal variables, then \(\sum_i Z_i^2\) has a chi-square distribution with \(k\) degrees of freedom.
tf.explanation: This is the construction of \(\chi_k^2\); its mean is \(k\) and its variance is \(2k\). Independence and unit normal scaling both matter.

tf.statement: For iid \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) observations with \(n\ge2\), \((n-1)S^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{n-1}\), where \(S^2=\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2/(n-1)\).
tf.explanation: Centering removes one orthogonal Gaussian coordinate, leaving the sum of squares of \(n-1\) independent standard normals. The factor is \((n-1)S^2/\sigma^2\), which also corrects the scaling typographical error on p.37.

tf.statement: If \(T\sim t_3\), its variance is one because it is a standardized ratio.
tf.explanation:
The slide gives \(\operatorname{Var}(T)=
u/(
u-2)\) for \(
u>2\). Thus \(t_3\) has variance \(3\), reflecting uncertainty in the random denominator.

mc.stem: Select every valid probability identity. Assume all conditional probabilities displayed are defined.

options.why: The final factor must condition on both earlier events: \(P(C\mid A\cap B)\). Conditioning only on \(B\) needs an additional conditional-independence assumption.

options.text: If \(A_1,A_2\) partition the sample space, then \(P(B)=P(B\mid A_1)+P(B\mid A_2)\).
options.why: The conditional terms must be weighted by \(P(A_1)\) and \(P(A_2)\).
The intersection is counted twice by the first two terms and must be subtracted once.
The denominator is the probability of the conditioning event \(B\).

mc.stem: Two independent fair bits \(U,V\) are drawn. Let \(A=\{U=1\}\), \(B=\{V=1\}\), and \(C=\{U=V\}\). Select every correct claim.

options.why: Both have probability \(1/2\) and their intersection has probability \(1/4\).
Their triple intersection has probability \(1/4\), whereas the product of the three probabilities is \(1/8\).
Conditioning on both bits being one forces them to be equal.

options.text: Pairwise independence always implies independence of every triple intersection.
options.why: This construction is pairwise independent, but its triple intersection fails the product rule for mutual independence.

mc.stem: A binary joint distribution is \(p(0,0)=0.30\), \(p(0,1)=0.10\), \(p(1,0)=0.20\), \(p(1,1)=0.40\). Select every correct conclusion.

options.why: Sum the joint probabilities across both values of \(Y\): \(0.20+0.40=0.60\).
Divide \(0.40\) by the marginal \(0.60\).
The product of marginals at \((1,1)\) is \(0.60\cdot0.50=0.30\), not \(0.40\).
The conditional probability is \(0.30/(0.30+0.20)=0.60\).

mc.stem: A joint density is \(p(x,y)=2\) on \(0<x<y<1\), and zero elsewhere. Select every correct statement.

options.why: The triangular support has area \(1/2\), so multiplying by two gives total mass one.
At a fixed \(x\), integrate \(2\) over \(x<y<1\).

options.text: \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent because their joint density is constant on its support.
options.why: The triangular support is not the product of the marginal supports. The joint density does not equal \(p_X(x)p_Y(y)\).
The marginal is \(p_Y(y)=2y\), giving conditional density \(1/y\) on \((0,y)\).

mc.stem: For a variable with finite second moment, select every correct moment formula.

options.why: Expand the centered square and use linearity.
The missing term is \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\), which need not be zero.
A constant shift vanishes after centering; the scale is squared.
Centering removes constants and multiplication contributes the product \(2(-1)\).

mc.stem: Let \(X\) take values \(-1,0,1\) with equal probabilities and let \(Y=X^2\). Select every correct claim.

options.why: Compute the finite sums over the three equally likely values.
Here \(E[XY]=E[X^3]=0\) and \(E[X]=0\), so the covariance is zero. The number \(2/9\) is the variance of \(Y\), not this covariance.
Knowing \(X=0\) forces \(Y=0\); \(P(Y=0\mid X=0)=1\ne1/3\).
Correlation requires positive variances, not nonzero means. Here \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=2/3\), \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2/9\), and the correlation is zero.

mc.stem: A count \(K\) records successes in \(20\) independent Bernoulli trials with success probability \(0.15\). Select every correct formula.

options.why: There are \(\binom{20}{2}\) disjoint placements of the two successes, each with the displayed product probability.
Add the expectations of the twenty success indicators.
Variance scales by the square of the divisor, so the variance is \(2.55/400\).

mc.stem: The counts \((N_1,N_2,N_3)\) come from \(10\) independent categorical trials with probabilities \((0.2,0.3,0.5)\). Select every correct statement.

options.why: The multinomial coefficient counts distinct arrangements of the category outcomes.
Each trial contributes to exactly one category count.

options.text: \(N_1,N_2,N_3\) are independent because the ten trials are independent.
options.why: The fixed total couples the category counts. For example, \(N_1=10\) forces \(N_2=0\).
Each marginal count is binomial with ten trials; a Bernoulli variable only takes values zero and one.

mc.stem: Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be iid with mean \(7\) and finite variance \(9\). Select every justified conclusion.

options.why: This is the weak law of large numbers under the supplied assumptions.
The central limit theorem approximates the centered and scaled mean by a standard normal.
The assumptions do not say the observations are normal; the central limit theorem supplies an asymptotic approximation.
The variance of the sum is \(9n\), so dividing by \(n^2\) gives \(9/n\).

mc.stem: For iid \(X_i\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), \(n\ge3\), let \(S^2=\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2/(n-1)\). Select every correct distribution statement.

options.why: A normalized linear combination of independent normal variables is exactly standard normal.
The correct residual sum is \((n-1)S^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{n-1}\).
They depend on disjoint coordinates after an orthogonal transformation of the standardized Gaussian sample.
The residual sum of squares has \(n-1\) degrees of freedom, so the ratio has distribution \(t_{n-1}\).

mc.stem: Let \(T\sim t_5\) and \(W=4+2T\). Select every correct claim.

options.why: The mean of \(t_5\) exists and is zero.
The scale parameter squared is four, but \(\operatorname{Var}(T)=5/3\), so \(\operatorname{Var}(W)=20/3\).

options.text: \(W\) has a general t distribution with location \(4\) and scale \(2\).
options.why: This is the location and scale transformation in the general t density.

options.text: \(T\) is exactly standard normal because its degrees of freedom exceed two.
options.why: The t distribution approaches the standard normal as degrees of freedom grow; finite degrees of freedom retain heavier tails.

mc.stem: A nonsingular bivariate Gaussian has mean \((1,-2)^T\) and covariance \(\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&9\end{pmatrix}\). Select every correct statement.

options.why: They are jointly Gaussian with zero covariance, so the joint density factors.
The determinant is \(36\), whose positive square root is six.
The inverse covariance is diagonal with entries \(1/4\) and \(1/9\).

options.text: The density at its mean equals the probability that the vector equals its mean.
options.why: The density at the mean is \(1/(12\pi)\), while the probability of that exact point is zero.

long.title: Deriving total probability, Bayes' rule, and posterior odds

parts.question: Let \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\) be a finite partition with \(P(A_i)>0\). Starting from disjoint events and the product rule, derive a formula for \(P(B)\). State the additional condition needed to condition on \(B\).
parts.solution: The events \(B\cap A_i\) are disjoint and their union is \(B\). Therefore \[P(B)=\sum_{i=1}^kP(B\cap A_i)=\sum_{i=1}^kP(B\mid A_i)P(A_i).\] To condition on \(B\), require this sum, and hence \(P(B)\), to be positive.

parts.question: Use the result to derive \(P(A_i\mid B)\), and prove that these posterior probabilities sum to one.
parts.solution: By conditional probability and the product rule, \[P(A_i\mid B)=\frac{P(A_i\cap B)}{P(B)}=\frac{P(B\mid A_i)P(A_i)}{\sum_jP(B\mid A_j)P(A_j)}.\] Summing the numerators over \(i\) reproduces the common positive denominator, so the posteriors sum to one.

parts.question: For two hypotheses \(H_1,H_0\) with positive priors, derive posterior odds after observing events \(E\) and \(F\). Assume the relevant likelihoods are positive. Show when the evidence contribution factors into \(P(E\mid H_i)P(F\mid H_i)\).
parts.solution: Cancel the common evidence denominator in Bayes' rule to obtain \[\frac{P(H_1\mid E\cap F)}{P(H_0\mid E\cap F)}=\frac{P(H_1)}{P(H_0)}\frac{P(E\cap F\mid H_1)}{P(E\cap F\mid H_0)}.\] The conditional product rule gives \(P(E\cap F\mid H_i)=P(E\mid H_i)P(F\mid E,H_i)\). If \(E\) and \(F\) are conditionally independent given each hypothesis, this becomes \(P(E\mid H_i)P(F\mid H_i)\). Thus posterior odds equal prior odds times two likelihood ratios. Unconditional independence of the two observations is not a substitute for this assumption.

long.title: Variance formulas and the effect of shared noise

parts.question: For finite-second-moment variables, derive \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y]\) and the variance of \(aX+bY+c\).
parts.solution: Writing \(\mu_X=E[X]\) and \(\mu_Y=E[Y]\), expansion yields \(E[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)]=E[XY]-\mu_X\mu_Y\). Also \(aX+bY+c-E[aX+bY+c]=a(X-\mu_X)+b(Y-\mu_Y)\). Squaring and taking expectations gives \[\operatorname{Var}(aX+bY+c)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)+b^2\operatorname{Var}(Y)+2ab\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y).\]

parts.question: Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) have common mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2\). Derive the mean and variance of \(\bar X_n\) in terms of all pairwise covariances. Specialize to independent observations.
parts.solution: Linearity gives \(E[\bar X_n]=\mu\). Expanding the centered sum gives \[\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)=\frac{1}{n^2}E\!\left[\sum_i(X_i-\mu)\sum_j(X_j-\mu)\right]=\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i,j}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).\] Equivalently it is \(\sigma^2/n+(2/n^2)\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)\). Under independence, each off-diagonal term is zero, so \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)=\sigma^2/n\). Identical means alone do not eliminate these terms.

parts.question: Suppose measurements have the form \(X_i=\mu+B+\epsilon_i\), where \(B,\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_n\) are independent, centered, and have variances \(\tau^2,\sigma_\epsilon^2,\ldots,\sigma_\epsilon^2\). Derive \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)\) and explain why the iid variance formula would fail.
parts.solution: We have \(\bar X_n=\mu+B+n^{-1}\sum_i\epsilon_i\). Independence gives \[\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)=\tau^2+\frac{\sigma_\epsilon^2}{n}.\] Alternatively, each individual variance is \(\tau^2+\sigma_\epsilon^2\), and every distinct pair has covariance \(\tau^2\), which gives the same result in the formula above. The measurements share \(B\) and are not independent. Averaging removes the independent noise component but leaves the positive variance floor \(\tau^2\).

long.title: Constructing the binomial distribution from trials

parts.question: Let \(I_1,\ldots,I_n\) be independent Bernoulli variables with common success probability \(p\in(0,1)\). For \(K=\sum_i I_i\), derive \(P(K=k)\) by counting disjoint outcomes.
parts.solution: A fixed ordered sequence containing \(k\) successes and \(n-k\) failures has probability \(p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\) by independence. Choosing the \(k\) success positions gives \(\binom nk\) disjoint sequences. Therefore \[P(K=k)=\binom nkp^k(1-p)^{n-k},\qquad k=0,\ldots,n.\]

parts.question: Derive the mean and variance of one Bernoulli variable directly from its two possible values. Then derive \(E[K]\) without differentiating a generating function.
parts.solution: For an indicator \(I\), \(E[I]=0(1-p)+1p=p\), and \(I^2=I\), so \(\operatorname{Var}(I)=E[I^2]-(E[I])^2=p-p^2=p(1-p)\). Linearity then gives \(E[K]=\sum_iE[I_i]=np\); this expectation calculation alone does not need independence.

parts.question: Derive \(\operatorname{Var}(K)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(K/n)\). Identify precisely where independence is used, and state the variance formula if the indicators are dependent but retain the same marginal success probability.
parts.solution: Expand the centered square: \[\operatorname{Var}(K)=\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(I_i)+2\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{Cov}(I_i,I_j).\] Independence implies \(E[I_iI_j]=p^2\), so the cross covariances vanish and \(\operatorname{Var}(K)=np(1-p)\). Scaling by \(1/n\) gives \(\operatorname{Var}(K/n)=p(1-p)/n\). With dependent indicators the general expression is \(np(1-p)+2\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{Cov}(I_i,I_j)\); the binomial pmf is also no longer guaranteed.

long.title: An exact Gaussian mean and residual decomposition

parts.question: Let \(X_i\) be iid \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), \(\sigma>0\), \(n\ge2\), and set \(Z_i=(X_i-\mu)/\sigma\). Choose an orthogonal matrix \(A\) whose first row is \((1,\ldots,1)/\sqrt n\), and let \(Y=AZ\). Using the joint standard normal density, prove that the coordinates of \(Y\) are independent standard normals.
parts.solution: The independent standardized observations have joint density \((2\pi)^{-n/2}\exp(-z^Tz/2)\). Since \(z=A^Ty\), \(z^Tz=y^Ty\) and the absolute Jacobian determinant is \(|\det A^T|=1\). Thus \[p_Y(y)=(2\pi)^{-n/2}e^{-\sum_jy_j^2/2}=\prod_{j=1}^n\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-y_j^2/2}.\] This factorization proves that the coordinates are iid standard normal. The first row has norm one because its entries are \(1/\sqrt n\).

parts.question: Express \(\sqrt n(\bar X-\mu)/\sigma\) and \(\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2/\sigma^2\) using these coordinates. Derive the chi-square law and prove independence of the sample mean and sample variance.
parts.solution: The first coordinate is \(Y_1=n^{-1/2}\sum_iZ_i=\sqrt n(\bar X-\mu)/\sigma\). The residual identity is \[\frac{\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2}{\sigma^2}=\sum_i(Z_i-\bar Z)^2=\sum_iZ_i^2-n\bar Z^2=\sum_{j=2}^nY_j^2.\] The last sum is \(\chi^2_{n-1}\), since it contains \(n-1\) independent squared standard normals. It is a function only of \(Y_2,\ldots,Y_n\), and hence is independent of \(Y_1\). The sample mean is a function of \(Y_1\); \(S^2\) is a function of the remaining coordinates. They are independent.

parts.question: For \(S^2=\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2/(n-1)\), derive the exact distribution of \(\sqrt n(\bar X-\mu)/S\). Explain why the same exact assertion does not follow merely from iid sampling with finite variance.
parts.solution: Let \(U=(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2=\sum_{j=2}^nY_j^2\). Then \(U\sim\chi^2_{n-1}\) and \(U\) is independent of \(Y_1\sim N(0,1)\). Therefore \[\frac{\sqrt n(\bar X-\mu)}{S}=\frac{Y_1}{\sqrt{U/(n-1)}}\sim t_{n-1}.\] For general iid finite-variance data, the normal-coordinate density factorization and exact chi-square residual law need not hold. The central limit theorem gives asymptotic normal behavior for a standardized mean, not this finite-sample t law.

long.title: Two inspections and the base rate of defective components

parts.question: A manufacturer draws components from a stable production stream. A component is defective with probability \(0.03\). One inspection flags a defective component with probability \(0.90\), and flags a nondefective component with probability \(0.04\). Compute the flag probability and the probability a flagged component is defective.
parts.solution: Let \(D\) denote a defect and \(F\) a flag. Total probability gives \(P(F)=0.90(0.03)+0.04(0.97)=0.0658\). Bayes' rule gives \[P(D\mid F)=\frac{0.027}{0.0658}=\frac{135}{329}\approx0.410334.\] Even with high sensitivity, nondefective components are common enough to contribute substantial false flags.

parts.question: The component is inspected twice. Assume the inspection outcomes are independent conditional on whether that component is defective, with the same sensitivity and false-flag probability each time. Compute the probability of two flags and the defect probability given two flags. Explain the factorization you used.
parts.solution: Conditional independence gives \(P(F_1\cap F_2\mid D)=0.90^2\) and \(P(F_1\cap F_2\mid D^c)=0.04^2\). Thus \[P(F_1\cap F_2)=0.03(0.81)+0.97(0.0016)=0.025852,\] and \[P(D\mid F_1\cap F_2)=\frac{0.0243}{0.025852}=\frac{6075}{6463}\approx0.939966.\] We factor within each defect class; the two flag events need not be independent without conditioning.

parts.question: A separate batch contains \(200\) independently drawn components, each inspected once, with independent inspection noise across components. Let \(K\) be its flag count. State its exact distribution, mean, variance, and the variance of its flag fraction \(K/200\).
parts.solution: Each flag indicator is Bernoulli with probability \(q=0.0658\), and the stated assumptions make the indicators independent. Hence \(K\sim\operatorname{Bin}(200,0.0658)\), \(E[K]=200q=13.16\), and \[\operatorname{Var}(K)=200q(1-q)=12.294072.\] The fraction has variance \(12.294072/200^2=0.0003073518\). Its mean is \(q\), not the underlying defect probability \(0.03\).

long.title: Exact inference for a normally distributed calibration error
long.source: PDF pp.31-37; interval construction is a supplemental application of the lecture pivots

parts.question: Nine independent calibration measurements, in millimeters, are \[498,\ 502,\ 501,\ 499,\ 500,\ 503,\ 497,\ 500,\ 500.\] Assume an iid \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) model with both parameters unknown. Compute \(\bar x\), the residual sum of squares, the unbiased sample variance \(s^2\), and the estimated standard error of the mean.
parts.solution: The deviations from \(500\) are \(-2,2,1,-1,0,3,-3,0,0\), which sum to zero. Thus \(\bar x=500\) and the squared deviations sum to \(4+4+1+1+0+9+9=28\). Therefore \(s^2=28/8=3.5\) square millimeters, and \(s/\sqrt9=\sqrt{3.5}/3\approx0.623610\) millimeters.

parts.question: Compute the t statistic for the target mean \(\mu_0=499\). Using \(t_{8,0.975}=2.306\), derive and calculate a central \(95\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu\). State the exact sampling assumption behind this interval.
parts.solution: The observed statistic is \(t=(500-499)/(\sqrt{3.5}/3)=3/\sqrt{3.5}\approx1.603567\). Under the normal model, \(T=\sqrt9(\bar X-\mu)/S\sim t_8\). The probability statement \(P(-2.306\le T\le2.306)\approx0.95\), with rounding in the quantile, rearranges to \[\bar X-2.306\frac{S}{3}\le\mu\le\bar X+2.306\frac{S}{3}.\] Substitution yields \(500\pm1.438044\), or approximately \([498.561956,501.438044]\) millimeters. Exact t coverage requires iid normal observations; finite variance by itself is insufficient.

parts.question: For the reference variance \(\sigma_0^2=4\), compute the chi-square statistic. Use \(\chi^2_{8,0.025}=2.180\) and \(\chi^2_{8,0.975}=17.535\) to derive and calculate a central \(95\%\) confidence interval for \(\sigma^2\).
parts.solution: The observed chi-square statistic is \((9-1)s^2/\sigma_0^2=28/4=7\). For the unknown true variance, \(U=8S^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_8\). Inverting \(2.180\le8S^2/\sigma^2\le17.535\) reverses the corresponding reciprocal inequalities and gives \[\frac{8S^2}{17.535}\le\sigma^2\le\frac{8S^2}{2.180}.\] The interval is \([28/17.535,28/2.180]\approx[1.596806,12.844037]\) square millimeters. The coverage is approximately \(95\%\) because the supplied quantiles are rounded.
